name: Macadamia oil

card.summary: A palmitoleic- and oleic-rich nut oil used as a cosmetic emollient and cooking oil, with composition research but no clear human skin-appearance trials.
card.note: Nut allergy is a consideration for any macadamia-derived product.

quick.overview:
Macadamia oil is pressed from the kernels of Macadamia integrifolia and related trees native to eastern Australia. It is mostly monounsaturated, with oleic acid and an unusual amount of palmitoleic acid, and it is used both in cooking and as an emollient in skin and hair products.

Research in the sources covers its fatty acids, oxidative stability and effects of dietary palmitoleic acid on blood lipids. No published human trial was found testing it on skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: As a topical ingredient it works as an emollient and fragrance fixative. Its low polyunsaturated content is linked to good oxidative stability. Palmitoleic acid has been studied in diet and metabolism research, not in skin-care trials.
quick.risks: Sources do not describe specific topical safety data. As a tree-nut product it can matter to people with nut allergy, a general consideration rather than a finding in the supplied studies.

lead: Macadamia oil is a non-volatile oil pressed from the kernels of the macadamia tree, chiefly Macadamia integrifolia, a species native to Australia and now grown commercially.[1] It is mostly monounsaturated: oleic acid is the main fatty acid, and palmitoleic acid, unusual in plant oils, is also present in notable amounts.[1]

It is used as a frying and salad oil and in cosmetics, where it serves as an emollient and fragrance fixative.[1] Research involving it covers composition across cultivars and oxidative stability; studies of palmitoleic acid look at blood lipids and metabolism rather than skin.[3][4][5] No clinical studies of its effect on human appearance were found.
infobox: Clear, light amber, slightly nutty odour[1]

paras: Reference sources give oleic acid as the dominant fatty acid, with palmitoleic acid at roughly a fifth of the oil by one estimate, linoleic acid around 1 to 3 percent and alpha-linolenic acid 1 to 2 percent; exact ranges differ between sources.[1][2] A comparison of oils from 15 cultivars grown in China found differences in composition and antioxidant capacity.[3] Studies on the oxidative stability of culinary oils include macadamia among the oils examined.[5] The low polyunsaturated content is linked to the oil's stability.[1]

In cosmetics the oil is used as an emollient and fragrance fixative.[1] As a food it is used for frying and, more often unheated, in dressings.[1] A Grokipedia entry attributes moisture-retention and wrinkle-reduction figures to cosmetic formulations containing the oil; that claim comes from an AI-generated source and was not matched to a trial in the supplied literature.[2]

Because macadamia oil is a source of palmitoleic acid, studies of that fatty acid are sometimes associated with it. A controlled diet study in hypercholesterolemic men compared palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids on plasma lipids,[6] and animal studies examined its effects on lipoproteins in hamsters and on metabolic syndrome in rats.[7][8] A review discussed palmitoleate and glucose homeostasis.[4] These concern dietary intake, not topical use.

The macadamia tree is native to Australian rainforests, and the oil's use as a commercial product follows the spread of cultivation of the nut.[1][2] Grokipedia states that Indigenous Australians used the nuts as food and oil as a liniment, and that seeds were taken to Hawaii in the 1880s; these details come from a single AI-generated source.[2]

No studies found on macadamia oil applied to skin or hair. Registered trials only loosely related to the oil include a study of dietary macronutrients on digestive and cardiovascular health (n=24)[9] and a trial of a vegetable-oil nutritional supplement in people at risk of diabetes (n=25).[10] Their results were not available among the sources, and they do not test topical or cosmetic use.
